I read this book several years ago, when it first came out and my son’s high school made it recommended reading for its students, something that I’m 100% sure would not happen today. It told the story (ostensibly a biography) of a kid from difficult circumstances in Appalachia who made it to Yale Law School. That’s before Vance decided to get involved in politics, after failing in venture capital. Looking at it today, he so inflates his resume that it makes me wonder weather anything in the book is factual. For example, he constantly talks about being a Marine in Iraq, as if he were dodging bullets in foxholes. In fact, he was refining his ability to spin stories to the press, working as an assistant in the Marine press office, far from the front lines. He briefly worked in “private equity” and formed his own private equity fund at one point, but the performance of his fund was dismal. He did benefit from it by being introduced to some billionaire investors who have used him to advance their own self-interests. It’s true that he was a Senator from Ohio, elected with the help of those same billionaires, but only for a few months before being selected to run for VP, whereupon he began worshipping the same man who he had spoken negatively repeatedly previously. He hardly graced the Senate floor, let alone learned anything from teh experience. He apparently did go to Yale; I have two Ivy League degrees and I can assure you that an Ivy League degree is far from endorsement of one’s intelligence or, even more so, integrity.

Rarely have we had a less qualified or experienced Vice President. Yet, the actuarial tables tell us that a 78-year old man of average health has about a 25% chance of dying within the next four years, so Vance has at least a 25% chance of being our next President.

Don’t waste your time or money on this book. Harry Potter is better fiction.

His Ivy League school years replaced what good common sense logic he had acquired and replaced it with a feeling that he was better than others and that if you can’t do what he did, you’re a failure & feeling sorry for himself when there was nothing to feel sorry for. Self-pity does not look good on you Mr. Vance. So many people face much more adversity in their life (e.g. Barack Obama — poor, mixed race, no father figure & looking black in a white dominated country,) and yet he came away from that experience, positive, hopeful with empathy and compassion, whereas Vance came away with arrogance and disdain. If so, he would’ve clearly pointed a few fingers at the wealthiest of Americans who were benefactors of the irreparable damage done to the Appalachian region. But don’t look here for any in-depth analysis; only woe is me and I’m so great to have overcome. As a book, it’s a disappointment at best; an embarrassment at worst.

When J. D. Vance was chosen as a vice-presidential candidate, I was curious to know more about him. I learned he had written a highly regarded autobiographical-sociological book about the woes of the impoverished and decaying industrial region where Vance was born and grew up.

Having raised my expectations, the book began with ten pages of favorable reviews. TEN PAGES. Everything from the NYTimes to Bustle, Goop, and the Daily Beast. That seemed extremely odd -- as if the publisher hoped I would feel only favorable opinions would be possible.

I got through three chapters with increasing dismay. Vance is a sloppy writer, disorganized, repetitive, and given to telling his readers things that are so obvious that one would think he had neither a good education nor a competent, demanding editor. He has no insights worthy of mention, but thinks it useful to let us know when a middle school or high school opened, where a rich family had their house, when a city tennis court lacked maintenance.

So, if he is a poor writer, do we value this as a life story? Perhaps, with editing, it could be a life story. I suspect that would be ineresting. Vance, immured in poverty, joined the Marines after high school, rose to the rank of corporal while doing public relations work, including a bit in Iraq. He then went to Ohio State, known for football, less for academic prowess. Then, amazingly, to Yale Law School, and to wealth as an investor with a venture capital firm. How could this be? That would be worth learning.

On the whole, I found this a whiny book, constant efforts at pontificating like a veteran sociologist, and ample evidence of a mediocre mind.

One thing I did find enlightening for anyone trying to fathom Vance's shift from denigrating Trump to idolizing the ex-president -- is that for which I have supplied an image.

Borrow a copy -- but don't waste your money and don't trust the prestigious (or the obscure) reviewers. I doubt they actually read the book.
